title: Bonuses where the City is a main funder
question: Where City payments were a quarter or more of an organization’s revenue, which listed officers and staff were paid a bonus that year, and how large was it against base pay?
finding: 186 bonus or incentive payments, $4.6 million in all, were reported by 38 organizations in tax years when City payments were a quarter or more of their revenue. The largest is $198,400 on base pay of $407,517 (Karen J Hanrahan, President/CEO (Thru 2/23), Glide Foundation, year ended 30 June 2023, when the City supplied 33% of revenue). In 8 cases the bonus was half of base pay or more. The organizations reporting most are Low Income Investment Fund (21), Meals On Wheels (19), Larkin Street Youth Services (14) and Safe & Sound (13). The Controller’s cost rules for nonprofit contracts list “Bonuses paid to staff.” among costs that may not be charged to the City, so a bonus at a City-funded organization has to be paid from other money; the returns do not show which money paid it.
how: The payments of the previous table, kept where the bonus came from the filing organization itself and City payments in the tax year were at least 25% of the revenue on the same return. Bonuses paid only by a related organization are left to the table on related organizations. For the two largest child-care voucher agencies the City figure is taken from the child-care pages, because the nonprofit-payments file leaves out most of what they are paid. “Bonus against base pay” divides the bonus column by the base-pay column of the same schedule. Largest first. Where the organization’s tax number was matched by hand and has not been verified, the last column says so.
limits: Some of these are plainly one-time: a payment on leaving labelled as a bonus, a retention payment through a change of leader, or a payout under a multi-year plan. At a lender or a development organization, incentive pay tied to loans made or money raised is a normal way to pay staff. The question a funder can fairly ask is what the bonus was tied to, and whether any of it was charged to a City contract, which the City’s rules do not allow. The compensation schedule (Schedule J) follows from the return’s question whether any listed person was paid more than $150,000, so bonuses to people below that line, and at organizations where nobody reaches it, are not on any return. The bonus column is defined by the tax form as bonus and incentive pay; organizations differ in what they put there, and some record a retention payment, a signing payment or a payout under a long-term plan in it.
